paper_title: A Foundation Model to Measure and Predict Human Behaviour

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to infer psychological attributes, predict individual behaviour, and simulate human populations. However, despite generating plausible responses, they often misrepresent individuals and distort population statistics. Here we introduce Chiron, a foundation model to measure and predict human behaviour. We jointly fine-tune an LLM to represent psychological constructs, predict individual behaviour, and align population response distributions with human statistics. The training and evaluation data span 36 behavioural domains and 78 social science experiments, comprising 288,307 person records, 1,411,750 atomic behavioural decisions, and 99,953 psychometric assessments over 109 psychological constructs. In our evaluations, Chiron's psychological measurements agree more closely with human self-reports and exhibit fewer biases that undermine psychometric validity. It predicts individual behaviour more accurately than frontier LLMs (up to 28.4% relative improvement). In simulations of social science experiments, it more accurately captures the direction and magnitude of human experimental effects (82.2--94.3% lower effect-size estimation error). Together, these results establish Chiron as a unified computational instrument for measuring and predicting human behaviour.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: A central goal of psychology and the behavioural sciences is to understand how people differ and how these differences shape behaviour across situations [Cronbach and Meehl, 1955]. Psychological measurement draws on what people say and do to infer latent attributes such as personality traits, values, and affective states, making subjective inner experience explicit and comparable across individuals [Demszky et al., 2023]. Behavioural prediction uses the available evidence to anticipate how individuals and populations will respond in new situations. Together, measurement and prediction provide complementary foundations for modelling human behaviour, linking interpretable psychological constructs with empirical predictive power [Hofman et al., 2021]. Recent work has begun to use large language models (LLMs) across these tasks, deploying them both as analytical instruments to infer psychological attributes from digital traces [Peters and Matz, 2024, Wright et al., 2026, Ziems et al., 2024] and as simulated research subjects to predict behaviour and replicate surveys or experiments [Aher et al., 2023, Argyle et al., 2023]. However, off-the-shelf LLMs often generate fluent, plausible responses that misrepresent individual differences and distort population statistics, raising several foundational challenges across psychology and computational social science. (1) Unstructured psychological assessments suffer from systematic psychometric biases. When prompted to score psychological attributes from text, general-purpose LLMs inflate socially desirable traits, compress inter-individual score dispersion, and shift estimates under superficial changes in prompt framing [Abdurahman et al., 2024, Brickman et al., 2025, Ye et al., 2025b]. (2) Psychological construct interpretability is disconnected from individual behavioural prediction. Existing approaches either extract trait scores without verifying out-of-sample predictive power [Zhu et al., 2025] or fine-tune black-box predictors without grounding representations in interpretable constructs [Binz et al., 2025, Xie et al., 2025]. Moreover, unadapted LLMs struggle to infer individuals distinctive values from their statements [Jiang et al., 2025], flatten within-group diversity into demographic stereotypes [Wang et al., 2025], and compress the linguistic diversity that reflects different individual traits [Sourati et al., 2026]. (3) Simulated populations exhibit homogenization and variance collapse. At the population level, LLM-based simulations cluster around stereotypical or modal responses [Kozlowski and Evans, 2025]. While simulated cohorts often recover the qualitative direction of experimental treatments, they systematically underestimate within-condition human variance. Consequently, these simulations severely exaggerate standardized effect magnitudes [Ashokkumar et al., 2026], often yield false positives on null findings [Cui et al., 2025], and only weakly capture cross-national variations in human preferences [Chen et al., 2026]. (4) Privacy and data-access constraints limit individual-level calibration. Adapting models to overcome these distortions requires rich behavioural supervision. However, raw human records paired with comprehensive psychometric annotations or participant-level experimental responses are rarely accessible at scale due to privacy and institutional constraints [Xu et al., 2026]. These failures stem from fundamental mismatch between the training objectives of general-purpose LLMs and the methodological requirements of behavioural science. Standard instruction tuning and preference optimization reward responses judged helpful, normative, or socially desirable by annotators, but do not require models to anchor internal representations in psychometric constructs, preserve idiosyncratic individual differences, or calibrate output distributions to human population variance. Aggregating feedback across annotators further privileges modal preferences at the expense of minority and individual perspectives [Conitzer et al., 2024, Santurkar et al., 2023, Sorensen et al., 2024]. Consistent with this mechanism, reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) reduces output entropy [Kirk et al., 2024] and collapses conceptual diversity in simulated populations [Murthy et al., 2025]. Addressing the challenges above therefore requires moving beyond zero-shot prompting of conversational chatbots toward foundation model explicitly architected and trained for psychometric validity, individual predictive fidelity, and distributional alignment. Here we introduce Chiron, foundation model to measure and predict human behaviour (Figs. 1 and 2). Chiron jointly learns psychological measurement, individual behavioural prediction, and population alignment within shared language model through three mechanisms. (1) decoupled latent readout estimates psychological constructs directly from person representations. Chiron attaches centred cosine measurement head to the hidden state at the end of persons observed records, scoring 109 psychological constructs without verbalized text generation and avoiding generative biases. (2) Joint psychometric supervision anchors individual behavioural prediction in latent construct representations. Measurement supervision across the 109 constructs directly shapes the shared person representation. The model then predicts individual behaviour from this structured psychological representation, linking interpretable traits with accurate behavioural prediction. (3) Constrained population synthesis calibrates the models response distribution to human experimental statistics. Because participant-level experimental data are rarely public, we synthesize virtual respondent cohorts whose answers match published condition means, standard deviations, and treatment effects. By training the model to generate diverse cohort responses for each experimental condition, Chiron counteracts variance collapse and reproduces human response distributions. We train Chiron on heterogeneous collection of questionnaire responses, personal writing, online posts, and experimental data. The combined training and evaluation data span 36 behavioural and psychological assessment domains and Figure 2: Overview of Chiron. single language model is jointly trained across three objectives: (1) psychological measurement, where construct scores supervise measurement head to estimate psychological attributes from personal records; (2) individual behavioural prediction, where answers withheld from persons records supervise the prediction of unseen responses and choices; and (3) population simulation, where virtual respondents synthesized to match published human statistics supervise the generation of population-level response distributions. 78 social science experiments, comprising 288,307 person records, 1,411,750 atomic behavioural decisions and 99,953 psychological scores spanning 109 psychological constructs. To overcome privacy and data-access barriers where raw human records or comprehensive annotations are unavailable, our training framework combines direct supervision from human records and psychometric assessments, self-supervised masked observation prediction on unlabelled personal writing, and calibrated synthetic supervision derived from psychometric item pools and published aggregate human statistics. We evaluate Chiron across psychological measurement, individual behavioural prediction, and population simulation. Its psychological measurements agree more closely with human self-reports across five datasets spanning nine constructs (mean Pearson = 0.390, compared with 0.3200.353 for frontier LLMs), while recovering empirical inter-construct correlations reported in the psychometric literature (r = 0.8060.819 across 150 construct pairs). Compared with frontier LLMs, Chiron substantially mitigates measurement biases (including score compression, irrelevant-context sensitivity, and evidence-order sensitivity), and responds monotonically to experimental manipulations of constructrelevant evidence across all 109 constructs. For individual prediction, Chiron predicts individual behaviour more accurately than frontier LLMs across 29 behavioural domains (mean prediction accuracy of 0.504 versus 0.3930.418, up to 28.4% relative improvement), generalizing both to unseen individuals and to held-out domains excluded from prediction training. For population simulations across 15 held-out experimental studies, Chiron preserves realistic within-condition dispersion and reproduces human experimental effects with 90.5% direction agreement and 82.294.3% lower effect-size estimation error (Cohens MAE of 0.224 versus 1.2543.895 for frontier LLMs). Together, these findings establish Chiron as unified computational instrument for measuring psychological attributes and predicting human behaviour at individual and population scales.

sections.title: 2 Related work
sections.content: Large language models are reshaping psychology and computational social science across multiple research roles, most notably as analytical assistants that extract psychological constructs from unstructured digital traces and as simulated research subjects that model individual decisions and collective experimental outcomes [Demszky et al., 2023, Xu 3 et al., 2026, Ziems et al., 2024]. Below, we situate Chiron within prior work on psychological measurement, individual behavioural prediction, and population simulation, highlighting how our unified training framework addresses recurring validity and fidelity challenges across these areas. Psychological measurement. Psychological measurement relates observable behavioural or linguistic evidence to latent constructs such as personality traits, values, and affective states [Cronbach and Meehl, 1955]. Moving beyond traditional self-report questionnaires and closed-vocabulary lexicon tools, recent studies prompt or adapt LLMs to infer dispositions from social-media posts, essays, and clinical narratives [Peters and Matz, 2024, Wright et al., 2026]. However, psychometric evaluations reveal substantial validity limitations in off-the-shelf LLMs: inferred scores often show modest agreement with self-reports [Zhu et al., 2025], exhibit systematic positivity and Western-centric biases [Abdurahman et al., 2024, Xu et al., 2026], compress inter-individual variance [Ye et al., 2025b], and shift under superficial changes in prompt wording, surrounding context, or evidence ordering [Brickman et al., 2025, Ye et al., 2025a]. Whereas general LLMs rely on autoregressive text generation to verbalize numerical ratings, Chiron introduces dedicated centred cosine readout head trained on multi-source psychometric supervision across 109 constructs, decoupling construct measurement from generative reporting biases. Individual behavioural prediction. growing literature seeks to predict how specific individuals will think, choose, or act across situations, which is prerequisite for reconciling explanatory psychological constructs with out-of-sample predictability [Hofman et al., 2021, Xu et al., 2026]. One approach supplies general-purpose LLM with personal context in the prompt: generative agents condition behaviour on memory streams [Park et al., 2023], and interviewgrounded agents use qualitative transcripts to emulate specific individuals [Park et al., 2024]. While rich personal context improves simulation plausibility, unadapted LLMs still struggle to infer an individuals underlying values and preferences from their own statements [Jiang et al., 2025] and often fall back on demographic or persona stereotypes [Wang et al., 2025, Xu et al., 2026]. complementary line of work fine-tunes foundation models directly on behavioural data: Centaur learns from trial-by-trial choices across cognitive psychology experiments [Binz et al., 2025], and Be.FM integrates experimental, survey, and literature data for behavioural prediction [Xie et al., 2025]. Chiron advances this paradigm in three ways: it generalizes prediction across heterogeneous personal records (combining questionnaires, essays, and social-media traces), introduces self-supervised masked observation prediction to leverage unlabelled personal writing at scale, and jointly supervises psychological measurement and behavioural prediction within shared representation space so that latent construct structure informs individual choice prediction. Population simulation. LLMs are also widely used as in silico research subjects to simulate survey populations [Argyle et al., 2023], replicate human-subject experiments [Aher et al., 2023, Ashokkumar et al., 2026, Cui et al., 2025], and probe strategic or social interactions [Akata et al., 2025, Kozlowski and Evans, 2025, Xu et al., 2026]. Despite their promise for pretesting experimental designs and exploring counterfactual scenarios, empirical audits consistently show that off-the-shelf LLMs suffer from variance compression and hyper-accuracy distortion [Kozlowski and Evans, 2025, Xu et al., 2026]: simulated samples suppress within-group heterogeneity [Santurkar et al., 2023, Wang et al., 2025], inflate standardized treatment effect sizes, produce false positives on null findings [Ashokkumar et al., 2026, Cui et al., 2025], and poorly reflect cross-national preference distributions [Chen et al., 2026]. Turning LLM simulations into reliable scientific instruments requires empirical calibration against observed human distributions, yet individual-level human responses are frequently unavailable due to privacy and institutional constraint [Xu et al., 2026]. Chiron addresses this bottleneck through constrained population synthesis, reconstructing respondent-level supervision from published aggregate human statistics so that the models conditional output distribution is directly aligned with empirical human means, variances, and treatment effects.

sections.title: 3 Methods
sections.content: To address the methodological challenges of using language models in behavioural science (e.g., construct invalidity, loss of individual heterogeneity, and population variance collapse), Chiron unifies psychological measurement, individual behavioural prediction, and population simulation within single foundation model  (Fig. 2)  . Human-authored text with self-reported assessments. We pair persons naturalistic essays, self-reflections, or social-media posts with psychometric scale scores completed by the same individual. Supervising the readout on self-reports grounds the models latent space in authentic human self-evaluations expressed through unstructured language. For multi-item human questionnaire datasets, the model receives subset of respondents item answers as input Rp, while the reference score tpc is calculated from disjoint held-out subset of items using the instruments official scoring and reverse-keying rules. Target scores are computed directly via the instruments scoring key, teaching the readout exact psychometric item keying and polarity. Synthetic narratives with comparison-derived scores. Each training instance pairs visible personal records Rp with one or more target questions q, supervised by the persons actual withheld answers across three data sources ( C.2): Recorded questionnaire answers, ratings, and choices. We introduce masked observation prediction, self-supervised task formulation that converts unlabelled personal narratives (e.g., from the Blog Authorship Corpus) into structured behavioural prediction instances at scale ( B.2). An extraction model first identifies high-confidence, quote-supported first-person observations regarding the authors recurring habits, interests, emotional patterns, and values. We hold out quarter of an authors extracted observations and transform each withheld observation into four-option question targeting either fine-grained behavioural distinction or an abstract dispositional tendency. Providing the remaining observations as Rp and training Chiron to recover the withheld choices teaches the model to perform multi-step behavioural inference from naturalistic personal evidence without human labels. We adapt Qwen3.6-35B-A3B [Qwen Team, 2026] using LoRA [Hu et al., 2022] and train the adapters and measurement head jointly for two epochs with λm = 8 and λp = 1 (full optimization hyperparameters in B.4). 3.4 Mechanistic and methodological advantages Chirons architecture and training design address fundamental limitations of both general-purpose LLMs and traditional psychological instruments. Mechanistic advantages over general-purpose LLMs. Off-the-shelf frontier LLMs are optimized for helpful, normative conversational assistance instead of scientific measurement or behavioural simulation. This creates three mechanistic failure modes that Chiron explicitly resolves: 1. Direct latent readout avoids the biases of verbalized scoring. When general LLMs are prompted to score psychological constructs in text, their outputs pass through the autoregressive token generation head, exposing estimates to RLHF-induced social desirability biases that inflate positive traits and compress score dispersion, as well as sensitivity to surrounding irrelevant context and prompt-order recency effects [Abdurahman et al., 2024, Xu et al., 2026, Ye et al., 2025b]. Chiron bypasses text generation entirely by mapping the person representation directly to continuous scores via dedicated measurement head (Eq. (1)) supervised on psychometric scales and balanced synthetic data. This architectural separation decouples psychological assessment from conversational text generation, avoiding the biases inherent to verbalized scoring. 8 2. Joint psychometric supervision structures person representations for behavioural prediction. Prior approaches either prompt general LLMs with personal context, which relies on surface lexical cues or demographic stereotypes [Jiang et al., 2025, Wang et al., 2025], or fine-tune black-box predictors without construct grounding, which can learn task-specific shortcuts that generalize poorly [Binz et al., 2025, Xu et al., 2026]. In Chiron, the measurement loss Lmeas supervises 109 psychological constructs directly on the shared hidden state hp, and the prediction loss Lpred conditions on this same state to predict withheld choices y. The measurement training thus regularizes hp to compress noisy personal records into stable dispositional dimensions that guide downstream prediction, while prediction training ensures that hp learns decision-relevant individual signals  (Fig. 5)  . 3. Distributional alignment counteracts mode collapse and restores population dispersion. Preference optimization of general LLMs concentrates models probability mass on modal responses [Kirk et al., 2024, Murthy et al., 2025, Santurkar et al., 2023]. In population simulation, this suppresses within-condition standard deviations, inflates standardized effect sizes, and produces false positives on null findings [Ashokkumar et al., 2026, Cui et al., 2025]. Chiron reverses this effect through constrained population synthesis and distributional alignment (Eqs. (4) and (5)). Training across the full cohort penalizes over-concentrated outputs and restores calibrated population distribution. Methodological advantages over traditional psychological tools. Compared with conventional psychometric questionnaires, laboratory experiments, and narrow text-analysis tools (such as lexicon dictionaries or single-trait classifiers), Chiron offers three distinct methodological advantages for behavioural science: 1. Unified, non-invasive assessment operates across heterogeneous evidence. Traditional psychometric scales require participants to complete fixed, structured item batteries, limiting sample scale and precluding retrospective measurement from naturalistic digital traces, historical texts, or qualitative interviews. Conversely, lexicon tools (e.g., word-count dictionaries) and task-specific classifiers are restricted to narrow trait sets and fail to capture compositional meaning or context. Chiron infers 109 standardized, theory-grounded constructs simultaneously from arbitrary mixtures of unstructured text, behavioural records, and questionnaire response. 2. Shared representations bridge construct interpretability and behavioural predictability. Psychological research has long faced divide between explanatory construct measurement (which yields interpretable trait profiles but often weakly predicts specific situational choices) and black-box behavioural prediction [Hofman et al., 2021, Xu et al., 2026]. By coupling an explicit 109-construct measurement head with generative behavioural predictor on the same person representation, Chiron provides both transparent psychological profiles and accurate predictions of individual behaviour. 3. Calibrated population simulation enables in silico pretesting of experimental designs. Conducting human-subject experiments across many candidate framing conditions, stimuli, or subpopulations is resource-intensive. While uncalibrated LLMs distort effect magnitudes, Chirons population alignment enables researchers to pretest experimental protocols, estimate plausible effect sizes and response distributions, and prioritize high-potential hypotheses in silico before deploying confirmatory human studies.

sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: We evaluate Chiron through psychological measurement, individual behavioural prediction, and population simulation. Measurement examines agreement with human assessments, alignment with literature-derived construct relationships, robustness to irrelevant changes, and responsiveness to experimental manipulations of construct-relevant evidence. Prediction tests responses withheld from personal records, while population simulation compares generated response distributions and experimental effects with human findings. All main evaluations use the same jointly trained model. Across all three evaluation settings, we compare Chiron with three frontier models (GPT-6 Sol, Claude Opus 5.5 and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash) and the unadapted Qwen3.6-35B-A3B base model. 4.1 Psychological measurement 4.1.1 Convergent validity Convergent validity measures the agreement between different assessments of the same psychological construct. We compare scores inferred from personal text with self-report assessments completed by the same authors, using Pearson correlation and mean absolute error (MAE). The evaluation spans five datasets (COVID-19 RW3D, Buechel empathy, PANDORA, PsihoRo and Student-SADD) covering nine constructs. Presented in Fig. 3a, we calculate Pearson correlation and MAE within each dataset and report the unweighted mean across datasets. For GPT-6 Sol, 127 requests that were refused after retries are excluded when computing its correlation and MAE. 9 Figure 3: Evaluation results of psychological measurement. a, Pearson and MAE against self-reports (five datasets, nine constructs). b, Construct correlations versus literature estimates (150 pairs, 60 constructs); dashed lines indicate = x. c, Standard deviation ratio of model scores to self-reports across five personality traits on PANDORA; 1 indicates equal dispersion. d, Absolute score changes under irrelevant-context perturbations (109 constructs). e, Absolute score changes under evidence-order perturbations (109 constructs). f, Stepwise monotonicity across four graded evidence levels (109 constructs). g, Direction accuracy for lowhigh evidence interventions on questionnaires, narratives and real records. 10 Chiron infers psychological constructs from personal text more accurately than frontier models. Across the five datasets, Chiron achieves mean Pearson of 0.390 and MAE of 0.398, outperforming all four baselines (r = 0.3200.353 and MAE = 0.5150.546). Detailed results by dataset and construct are presented in Table 7. 4.1.2 Nomological validity Nomological validity assesses whether relationships among measured constructs agree with established psychological theory and empirical findings [Cronbach and Meehl, 1955]. We examine this by calculating correlations among Chirons construct scores across individuals and comparing them against literature benchmark of median empirical correlations compiled from published psychometric studies. The evaluation covers 150 relationships among 60 constructs, assessed separately across three datasets with distinct record types: PAN15, Essays, and ESS09. The results are plotted in Fig. 3b. Benchmark construction and evaluation details provided in C.1.3. Chiron recovers empirical inter-construct relationships reported in the psychological literature. Across the three datasets, correlations among Chirons inferred scores align closely with literature benchmarks, reaching Pearson correlations of 0.816 on PAN15, 0.806 on Essays and 0.819 on ESS09, with sign agreement in 91.393.3% of construct pairs  (Table 8)  . This consistency across social-media posts, personal essays, and survey responses indicates that Chiron preserves coherent nomological structure across different forms of personal evidence. 4.1.3 Measurement bias Measurement bias refers to systematic distortions in inferred scores that are unrelated to the target construct. We examine three types of bias across Fig. 3ce: (1) score compression (Fig. 3c), whether inferred scores across individuals are compressed into narrower range than human self-reports, measured by the ratio of model-score standard deviation to self-report standard deviation averaged across the Big Five traits on PANDORA (where 1 indicates equal dispersion); (2) irrelevant-context sensitivity (Fig. 3d), whether scores drift when construct-irrelevant background statements in the input are replaced while the target evidence is held fixed, measured by the mean absolute score change (n = 543 units across all 109 constructs); and (3) evidence-order sensitivity (Fig. 3e), whether scores depend on record ordering, measured by the mean absolute score change when the presentation order of statements in an input is reversed (n = 540 units across all 109 constructs). Evaluation protocols and detailed results are provided in C.1.4. Chiron exhibits less score compression and greater invariance to irrelevant context and evidence ordering than baseline models. On PANDORA (Fig. 3c), all models are compressed relative to self-reports, but Chiron reaches mean standard-deviation ratio of 0.573, remaining closer to human dispersion than the three frontier models (0.3830.412) and the base model (0.523). The frontier models stronger compression relative to both Chiron and the base model corroborates the mechanism discussed in 3.4: post-training and preference alignment homogenize verbalized assessments toward modal values [Kirk et al., 2024, Murthy et al., 2025, Xu et al., 2026], whereas Chirons centred representation readout better preserves inter-individual dispersion. Under input perturbations (Fig. 3d,e), Chiron likewise achieves the smallest mean absolute score changes: 0.0238 when replacing construct-irrelevant context (versus 0.04330.0850 across baselines, reducing context-induced drift by 45.071.9%) and 0.0270 when reversing evidence order (versus 0.04330.1139 across baselines). 4.1.4 Experimental manipulation In psychometric validation, valid measurement instrument must respond predictably to experimental manipulations of construct-relevant evidence while holding background context constant. We conduct controlled interventions that systematically manipulate the diagnostic evidence for target construct across all 109 constructs: we progressively replace low-level evidence with high-level evidence across four graded levels in questionnaire and narrative inputs, and insert contrasting lowor high-level narratives into otherwise unchanged real personal records. We evaluate stepwise monotonicity as the proportion of adjacent transitions across the four graded manipulation levels in which the score strictly increases, and direction accuracy as the proportion of cases in which the high-evidence manipulation receives higher score than the low-evidence manipulation. The results are shown in Fig. 3f,g; experimental setups and detailed results are provided in C.1.5. Chiron responds monotonically and in the expected direction to experimental manipulations of construct-relevant evidence. Across all 109 constructs, Chirons scores strictly increase across 99.4% of adjacent steps for questionnaire evidence and 94.7% for narrative evidence, compared with 67.294.0% and 68.094.3% for the four baselines. For direction accuracy, Chiron reaches 100.0% on both questionnaire and narrative manipulations (versus 96.599.3% and 98.599.7% for the baselines) and 93.8% when contrasting narratives are inserted into real personal records (versus 87.696.4% for the baselines). Figure 4: Prediction accuracy across 29 behavioural domains. Bars show mean prediction accuracy (1 SEM) across test cases within each domain. 12 4.2 Individual behavioural prediction We evaluate whether Chiron can predict persons withheld responses, choices, or behavioural attributes, based on their available personal records. The benchmark spans 29 behavioural domains and examines two generalization settings: (1) held-out individuals, which tests unseen participants (or source records) across the 25 domains included in behavioural prediction training; and (2) held-out domains, which tests four additional domains excluded from behavioural prediction training (HEXACO, MACH-IV, RIASEC and SAPA-2022). All models receive the same observed records and target questions. The test set contains 4,767 cases: 3,967 cases in the 25 represented domains and 800 cases in the four held-out domains. We compute prediction accuracy for each test case (the proportion of withheld target questions answered correctly for that person) and report the mean and standard error of the mean (SEM) across cases within each domain. For GPT-6 Sol, 60 requests that were refused after retries are excluded when computing its mean accuracy, whereas malformed outputs (two Blog cases for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B) are scored as zero. Domain-level results across both generalization settings are presented in Fig. 4, with further details provided in C.2. Chiron more accurately predicts individual behavior, generalizing to both unseen individuals and unseen behavioural domains. Across all 29 domains, Chiron reaches mean prediction accuracy of 0.504 (averaging equally across domains), compared with 0.3820.418 for the four baselines, and ranks first in 28 of the 29 domains. This advantage holds across both generalization levels: on held-out individuals within the 25 represented domains, Chiron attains mean prediction accuracy of 0.522 (versus 0.3890.425 for the baselines), and on the four held-out domains excluded from prediction training, it remains the top-performing model on every domain with mean prediction accuracy of 0.391 (versus 0.3120.370). To examine how psychometric supervision and latent construct measurement support downstream behavioural prediction ( 3.4), we trace Chirons construct readouts at </person_records> and its item-level predictions across four graded evidence levels (L1L4) in two settings  (Fig. 5)  . (1) We conduct cross-domain counterfactual case study on naturalistic personal records (Fig. 5ad). Here, we hold three everyday routine notes fixed and progressively replace three unstructured habits in task scheduling, personal finances, and work organization with structured alternatives from L1 (0/3 structured) to L4 (3/3 structured) (Fig. 5a). Conditioning on the person representation at </person_records>, we read out Chirons construct scores (Fig. 5b) and compare expected, predicted option ratings E[y] = (cid:80)5 k=1 p(y = Rp, q) between Chiron and the unadapted Qwen3.6-35B-A3B base model. Two models predict item response on held-out vocational domain (Hollands RIASEC inventory, rating job activity Maintain employee records from 1 = Dislike to 5 = Enjoy; Fig. 5c) and reverse-keyed future-orientation item (Consideration of Future Consequences Scale, CFCS, only act to satisfy immediate concerns, figuring the future will take care of itself; Fig. 5d). (2) We extend the case study to systematic within-instrument test across all 109 constructs (Fig. 5e). For each construct, we pair each of five synthetic backgrounds with three item responses. Keeping the background fixed, we change these responses one at time from the lowestto the highest-scoring answer, creating four evidence levels (L1L4). For each input, Chiron measures the construct and predicts responses to three other target items. The five backgrounds and four levels yield 2,180 inputs and 6,540 item predictions across all constructs. Experimental setups and evaluation details are provided in C.2.3. Construct measurement and cross-domain prediction respond consistently to graded evidence. In the counterfactual case study, Chirons inferred conscientiousness increases monotonically across levels (0.33 0.02 +0.40 +0.89) alongside Hollands conventional vocational interest, which captures preference for orderly, rulegoverned clerical work (0.37 0.10 +0.33 +0.81). As comparison, an unrelated trait (extraversion) remains flat near zero (0.02 to +0.11). Given the same personal records, Chirons expected option ratings shift smoothly and monotonically on both the held-out RIASEC item (2.26 2.87 3.57 4.35; Fig. 5c) and the reverse-keyed CFCS item (3.69 2.88 1.79 1.49; Fig. 5d). By contrast, the unadapted Qwen3.6-35B-A3B base model fails to integrate graded behavioural evidence and exhibits pronounced extreme-option selection bias characteristic of general-purpose LLMs on Likert-type scales. Instead of calibrating intermediate ratings to mixed evidence, it collapses probability mass onto the scale endpoints (1 or 5), remaining near the floor on the held-out RIASEC item across L1L3 (1.12 1.11 1.25) before jumping abruptly to 4.96 at L4, and switching sharply between opposite extremes on the CFCS item (4.98 4.65 versus 1.24 1.00). Latent construct scores summarize the graded evidence behind within-instrument prediction. Across all 109 constructs in the systematic within-instrument test (Fig. 5e), Chirons construct scores and mean prediction scores increase together in 99.27% of adjacent transitions. To examine whether the construct score accounts for the prediction itself, we treat each constructs 20 records, formed by crossing its five backgrounds with the four evidence levels, as Figure 5: Linking latent construct measurement to behavioural prediction under graded evidence interventions. a, Counterfactual intervention on personal records: three fixed routine notes are paired with three daily-habit slots (scheduling, finances, and organization) that are progressively replaced from unstructured (L1, 0/3) to structured (L4, 3/3). b, Chiron measurement results across L1L4. c,d, Expected item ratings across L1L4 for Chiron and the base model on held-out vocational interest item (Holland RIASEC; c) and reverse-keyed future-orientation item (CFCS; d). e, measurement scores (x-axis) and target-item prediction score (y-axis) across four graded evidence levels (L1L4) for all 109 constructs (n denotes constructs per category; 2,180 inputs and 6,540 item predictions). Prediction scores average expected responses across three target items per construct, keyed toward the high pole and rescaled to [1, 1]. Thin lines trace individual constructs (averaged over five synthetic backgrounds); thick lines indicate category means. 14 separate observations. Within each construct, we first regress the mean prediction score on the construct score alone, and then repeat the regression after adding the evidence level, coded as 0, 1, 2 and 3. The construct score linearly explains the mean prediction score, with mean Pearson of 0.970 (R2 = 0.942) across constructs, and adding the evidence level increases R2 by only 0.007. The continuous readout therefore already summarizes the graded evidence on which the prediction depends. Figure 6: Population simulation across 15 held-out studies. a, Simulated versus human Cohens across 25 eligible effects from eight studies; the dashed line indicates = x. b,c, Effect-size estimation error (Cohens MAE, = 25) and response-distribution error (NMAE, = 34). df, Effect-direction accuracy (n = 42), effect-size Pearson correlation (n = 25), and statistical significance F1 (n = 53). Arrows indicate the preferred direction for each metric. 4.3 Population simulation We evaluate whether simulated populations reproduce human response distributions and experimental effects across social science experiments. The benchmark splits studies into 63 training studies and 15 held-out test studies; all conditions from study remain in the same split, and only training studies contribute to population synthesis and joint training. Across the 15 test studies, each model generates 4,277 planned virtual participants over 45 experimental conditions, following the replication protocol of Cui et al. [2025]. We apply each studys original scoring procedure to compare simulated and human outcomes in terms of effect magnitudes (Cohens MAE and Pearson correlation), effect direction accuracy, statistical significance F1, and normalized mean absolute error (NMAE) of response distributions. For Claude Opus 5.5, 98 refused requests are not imputed. GPT-6 Sol, Claude Opus 5.5 and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash each have one zero-variance condition pair in AMJ_4_2. Results across the 15 held-out studies are presented in Fig. 6, with further details provided in C.3. Chiron more faithfully reproduces human experimental effects and response distributions across held-out studies than frontier models. Across the 15 held-out studies, Chiron substantially outperforms all four baselines on four of the five evaluation metrics. For treatment effect estimation, Chiron reduces Cohens MAE to 0.224 (compared with 0.7983.895 for the baselines) and reaches an effect-size correlation of = 0.873 (versus 0.5400.703), while achieving 15 the highest effect direction accuracy at 90.5% (versus 78.683.3%). It also matches human response distributions more closely, with distribution NMAE of 0.0755 compared with 0.12480.1638 for the baselines. Notably, stronger frontier models exhibit larger distributional and effect-size distortions than the unadapted base model: Cohens MAE increases monotonically from 0.798 for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B to 1.2543.895 across the three frontier models, accompanied by parallel rise in distribution NMAE (with the three frontier models even collapsing to zero within-condition variance in AMJ_4_2). This pattern directly reflects the mechanism analysed in 1 and 3.4: standard instruction tuning and preference alignment suppress within-condition response variance and homogenize simulated participants, which systematically inflates standardized effect sizes (d, where between-condition mean differences are divided by pooled within-condition standard deviation). This mechanism also explains why Chiron obtains lower statistical significance F1 than the baselines (0.678 versus 0.7410.785 across the 53 tests). Because published experimental benchmarks consist predominantly of statistically significant findings (p < 0.05) and the F1 metric rewards true positives while ignoring true negatives, models that indiscriminately produce small p-values are systematically favoured. By underestimating within-condition variance and exaggerating treatment effects, the four baselines declare 1922 more comparisons statistically significant than Chiron, raising true positives from 20 to 2931 but correctly identifying only 25 true negatives on null human effects (compared with 14 for Chiron). In contrast, Chiron preserves realistic response dispersion and produces more conservative, better-calibrated effect magnitudes.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion and Discussion
sections.content: We introduced Chiron, foundation model to measure and predict human behaviour that jointly learns psychological measurement, individual behavioural prediction, and population alignment within shared language model. Combining psychometric supervision, self-supervised masked observation prediction, and constrained population synthesis enables scalable learning from heterogeneous individual records and aggregate study statistics. Across our evaluations, Chiron produces more accurate and psychometrically valid construct measurements than frontier LLMs, recovering literature-derived nomological networks while mitigating score compression, irrelevant-context drift, and evidence-order sensitivity. For individual prediction, Chiron outperforms frontier models across 29 behavioural domains (up to 28.4% relative improvement), generalizing to both unseen individuals and held-out domains. In population simulations across 15 held-out social science experiments, it counteracts the variance collapse of aligned frontier LLMs and reduces effect-size estimation error by 82.294.3%. Together, these findings establish Chiron as unified computational instrument for measuring psychological attributes and predicting human behaviour across individual and population scales. Towards addressing fundamental challenges for LLMs in computational social science. In 1, we outlined four methodological challenges that limit general-purpose LLMs in psychology and computational social science. Our empirical findings show promise for addressing each challenge: Decoupled latent readouts mitigate psychometric biases in unstructured assessment. Off-the-shelf LLMs suffer from social-desirability inflation, variance compression, and framing sensitivity when verbalizing psychological measurement through text generation [Abdurahman et al., 2024, Brickman et al., 2025, Ye et al., 2025b]. Chiron architecture measures constructs directly from person representations, bypassing token generation. This design yields closer agreement with human self-reports, alignment with literature-derived construct relationships, fuller inter-individual score dispersion, smaller drift under irrelevant context and evidence-order changes, and monotonic responses to experimental manipulations of construct-relevant evidence  (Fig. 3)  . Jointly learning construct readouts and behavioural prediction reconciles interpretability with predictability. Bridging explanatory psychological constructs and out-of-sample behavioural prediction has been longstanding challenge [Hofman et al., 2021]. Joint supervision on shared person representation yields transparent trait profiles and accurate predictions of withheld behavior  (Fig. 4)  . Trait scores and predicted item answers shift together when trait-related evidence strengthens  (Fig. 5)  , suggesting measurement and prediction draw on the same information. The same person representation thus links interpretable traits to the choices the model predicts. Distributional alignment mitigates homogenization and variance collapse in simulated populations. Heavily posttrained frontier LLMs often collapse within-condition variance and exaggerate standardized treatment effects in experimental simulation [Ashokkumar et al., 2026, Cui et al., 2025, Kozlowski and Evans, 2025]. Constrained population synthesis trains Chiron to match human statistics. It produces more realistic response distributions, better-calibrated effect magnitudes, and fewer false positives on null human findings  (Fig. 6)  . These results point toward the potential of using Chiron-driven simulations to pretest experimental designs, screen survey instruments, and gauge plausible effect sizes before confirmatory human studies. Self-supervision and synthetic data mitigate privacy and data-access constraints. Our results suggest that Chiron can be trained and calibrated without raw participant-level experimental releases or exhaustive psychometric labels on every record [Xu et al., 2026]. For measurement training, psychometrically labelled human text is scarce. We generate first-person stories for all 109 constructs and fits measurement supervision from pairwise-calibrated construct scores. For prediction training, masked observation prediction allows learning individual behaviour from unlabelled personal writing. For distributional alignment, constrained population synthesis fits virtual respondents to published human statistics. Limitations and future directions. We note several methodological scope boundaries and directions for extension. First, our measurement head uses fixed inventory of 109 constructs instead of open-ended trait descriptions. These 109 constructs are curated from established psychometric taxonomies  (Table 4)  to provide broad, non-redundant coverage across five core domains of human variation: personality and vocational interests, self-evaluation and interpersonal functioning, affect and mental health, moral and cultural values, and cognitive self-regulation. This inventory offers sufficient theoretical completeness to represent individual differences. Second, our behavioural prediction objective targets structured choices, ratings, and classifications rather than free-text generation. Focusing on structured decisions removes surface linguistic confounds, enables exact evaluation against human ground truth, and matches standard survey and experimental formats. Extending Chiron to open-ended dialogue and free-form behavioural generation is an important next step. Third, our model encodes persons records as static snapshot. Incorporating longitudinal timestamps will help separate stable traits from transient states over time. Ethical considerations. Models that infer psychological attributes and predict human behaviour carry dual-use risks that require clear boundaries. First, psychological inference from digital traces must respect informed consent and autonomy. Chiron is built for scientific research only, and must not be used for unauthorized profiling, covert surveillance, or high-stakes automated decisions in hiring, credit, insurance, or clinical diagnosis. Second, because inferring individual dispositions and framing effects could enable targeted persuasion or manipulation, personalized AI systems using psychometric representations require human oversight and safeguards against manipulative steering. Third, in population simulation, calibrated in silico cohorts are designed for hypothesis generation and experimental pretesting. Validation with real human subjects remains essential before drawing scientific conclusions.

Each definition describes the intended meaning of high construct score. The reference column identifies the conceptual basis, not necessarily the item instrument used in training or evaluation. Personality and vocational interests. IPIP and IPIP_NEO refer to the International Personality Item Pool, publicdomain item repository spanning personality, interpersonal, affective and cognitive scales [Goldberg et al., 2006, Oregon Research Institute, n.d.]; HEXACO to the HEXACO Personality Inventory [Lee and Ashton, 2004, n.d.]; SD3 to the Short Dark Triad [Jones and Paulhus, 2014]; and RIASEC to Hollands vocational interest model [Holland, 1997]. Self-evaluation and interpersonal attributes. RSES refers to the Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale [Rosenberg, 1965]; ECR to the Experiences in Close Relationships scale [Brennan et al., 1998]; and IRI to the Interpersonal Reactivity Index [Davis, 1983], whose Empathic Concern and Perspective Taking subscales capture affective and cognitive empathy. We construct the literature reference benchmark from large corpus of published psychometric research articles. Specially tailored LLM agents first parse these articles to identify psychological construct entities and their reported empirical relationships, followed by manual review to verify the extracted records. From this collection, we select entries that report Pearson correlation coefficients and map their construct entities onto Chirons 109-construct inventory. Construct alignment relies on scale names and common aliases, consulting construct definitions, item wording, and surrounding article context whenever the correspondence is ambiguous. Across the full inventory, this mapping yields 346 construct pairs spanning 92 constructs. For each pair, we aggregate multiple literature findings by taking the median reported correlation coefficient, and retain pairs supported by at least two empirical entries. This filtering produces the final benchmark of 150 reference relationships across 60 constructs, which is evaluated across all three datasets. Evaluation procedure and results. We evaluate these 150 relationships on three datasets with distinct record formats: PAN15 [Rangel et al., 2015] (577 author-profiling participants), Essays [Pennebaker and King, 1999] (2,467 personal essay authors), and ESS09 [European Social Survey, 2018] (4,921 survey respondents). Within each dataset, Chiron infers all 109 construct scores for each individual, and we compute the Pearson correlation across individuals for each of the 150 construct pairs. C.1.5 Experimental manipulation All three intervention settings follow the same experimental manipulation logic: we hold background context fixed and systematically manipulate construct-relevant evidence by replacing low-level evidence for target construct with high-level evidence, testing whether the inferred construct score increases accordingly. Graded interventions on questionnaires and narratives. For each of the 109 constructs, we construct four-level input series (six statements per input) by pairing three target statements with three fixed neutral background statements. Starting from Level 1 (all three target statements at the low level), we successively replace one, two and all three low-level target statements with their high-level counterparts (Levels 24), keeping the background statements and positions unchanged: Questionnaire evidence (n = 541 series; up to five per construct): each target statement is naturalized questionnaire item whose response is flipped from its low to its high endpoint (for example, changing know how to captivate people from Very inaccurate to Very accurate), producing four levels with mean target scores of 1, 1/3, 1/3 and 1. The three background statements are midpoint filler items from other constructs ( C.1.4). Narrative evidence (n = 325 series; up to three per construct): each lowhigh pair consists of two held-out synthetic narratives ( 3.3.1) with negative and positive BradleyTerry scores, matched in scenario, writing style, length and absolute intensity (for example, preferring quiet evening alone versus seeking out friends company for extraversion). The three background statements describe routine daily activities and are shared across constructs. Interventions on real personal records. To test whether single piece of contrasting evidence shifts scores in the expected direction against realistic personal history, we sample 200 personal-record backgrounds each from PANDORA, DASS and IPIP-FFM (n = 592 evaluated units). C.2.3 Detailed experimental setup for linking construct measurement to prediction We test whether Chirons construct measurements and predicted questionnaire responses change together when evidence about hypothetical person is varied (Fig. 5e). The experiment covers all 109 constructs. For each construct, we create records containing three fixed statements about everyday background and three responses to questionnaire items. The item responses describe different levels of the construct. For example, agreement with follow schedule provides evidence of higher conscientiousness. We make four versions of each record: at L1, all three responses indicate low construct levels; one response is switched to its high-level counterpart at each step, until all three indicate high levels at L4. For an item describing disorganized habits, disagreement supplies the high-conscientiousness response. For each of the 109 constructs, we combine five sets of background notes with four levels of construct-relevant evidence, yielding 2,180 input records. Three other items about the same construct are reserved as prediction questions. They never appear in that constructs input records and remain fixed across its backgrounds and evidence levels. The model predicts how the hypothetical person would answer each question, giving 6,540 item predictions. Of the 327 construct-specific target questions, 262 use existing questionnaire items, and the other 65 are written from construct definitions when existing items are not sufficient. We score its possible Option answers and normalize their probabilities over the listed options. The expected response is the probability-weighted mean of the option numbers. We linearly rescale this expectation to [1, 1], reversing items for which larger responses indicate less of the construct. Higher prediction scores therefore always indicate more of the target construct.
